svg.text: Inflection varies form within a class; derivation makes a new word, often new class.
Non-affixal (§4.2): conversion (to chair a meeting), clipping (photo), blending (brunch), back-formation (burgle), acronymy.
OPEN CLASSES — content words, take new members freely; head NP/VP/AdjP/AdvP (§3.1–3.5)
CLOSED CLASSES — fixed, small, grammatical function words (interjections sit awkwardly here)
† “Present Progressive” = “present continuous” (§4.3.2). H&P (CGEL): English has only two inflectional tenses — present, past.
VERB FORMS: FIVE FORMS, PARTICIPLES & PARADIGMS
Past pt. (written) → PERFECT: has written (§4.3.3) · PASSIVE: was written (§5.5.1) · past-ptcl. clause: Written quickly, it was flawed (§2.7)
Pres. pt. (writing) → PROGRESSIVE: is writing (§4.3.2) · participial phrase: the woman writing (§3.6)
“-ing” = one form, three jobs: Progressive (is running) · Gerund=noun (Swimming is fun, §3.8) · Pres. ptcl.=adj. (the dog running, §3.6)
Valency (§4.7): Intransitive — He slept. · Transitive — She read the book. · Ditransitive — She gave him the book.
Complex-trans. — They made him king. · Copular — She is a doctor.
Infinitive paradigm (§4.12): Bare — I heard him write. · To-inf. — She wants to write. · Perfect — He seems to have written it.
Progressive — She appears to be writing. · Perf.prog. — They seem to have been writing. · Passive — It needs to be written.
Particles & phrasal verbs (§4.5): a particle (up, down, off, out, on) binds to the verb — “give up” ≠ give + up.
Separability test: it may move past a noun object (“give the fight up”) and must follow a pronoun object (“give it up”, never “*give up it”) — this is what separates it from a preposition.
MODALITY — EPISTEMIC vs DEONTIC (two separate scales)
Certain inference — You must be tired.
Strong expectation — She should be home by now.
Weaker possibility — It might rain later.
Requirement — You must finish your homework.
Same modal, different meaning: “must” on the epistemic reading (inference) vs the deontic reading (requirement) are not one scale.
Modals are bare-infinitive auxiliaries (no -s/inf./pple, §4.8) preceding perfect/progressive in §3.2 order: “She might have been working.”
Semi-modals (have to, ought to, need to, be able to, used to) inflect normally and supply the forms modals lack.

NICE (§4.8): Neg. “is not”/“do not” · Inv. “Is he?”/“Do you?” · Code “so can he” · Emph. “does like it”. Stative/dynamic (§4.9): dynamic takes progressive (is running); stative resists it (know/own/seem).
Numerals: cardinal/ordinal — treated as determiners (classification contested, §4.4.5)
§5.2.1 · §5.2.2 — strong tendency, not absolute; slot 8 unfilled here (cf. a leather riding boot)
Source: Grammar_contents.md (Lukeatron Grammar parser aide). Section numbers (§) refer to that catalogue.
